title: The Cost of Finding the Keys
author: Tatra Labs

sections.value:
A coding agent that has been working for a day can carry millions of tokens of context: the
repository it has read, every command it ran and what it printed, the plan it has revised three
times. Each new token the model writes has to look back over all of it. That look-back is
attention, and at this length attention is the bill.

Sparse attention is the answer the field has been converging on. DeepSeek, Qwen, MiniMax and Z.ai have
all published designs in which a small, cheap *indexer* picks a few thousand keys for each query,
and the expensive attention reads only those. It works. In one such model, GLM-5.3-Flash, a sparse
attention layer prefills at 10 million tokens about **21×** faster than full attention would.

And **98%** of the time that remains goes to the indexer. The layer now spends almost nothing
reading the keys it needs, and almost everything deciding which ones they are.

[*Latent Sparse Attention: Towards Subquadratic Ultra-Long Context
Attention*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.42147), from Prefrontal AI in London and ETH Zurich
(Kubicek, Caciolai, Peng and seven co-authors, among them Torsten Hoefler and James Whittington;
30 October 2026), is about that 98%. Its idea is to stop scoring every key and to search clusters of
keys instead, the way a vector database searches an index rather than a table. The headline
numbers are large. At 10 million tokens, one attention layer becomes **22.7×** faster than
GLM-5.3-Flash's own sparse attention, and **72.4×** faster than full attention in Qwen-3.8-27B. The
full picture is more useful than the headline. End to end, the same change brings the first token
**2.2×** and **9.2×** sooner. Below a million tokens it buys roughly nothing, and in some
configurations it costs a little.

This post works through why the search became the bottleneck, how LSA restructures it, what the
measurements show, and where they stop.

## Sparse attention moved the cost

In full attention every query is compared with every key before it. Prefilling a context of T
tokens costs on the order of T², so ten times the context is a hundred times the work, and each
token decoded afterwards costs on the order of T. At ten million tokens the quadratic term is the
whole story.

Sparse attention rests on an empirical fact: a query needs very few of those keys. The LSA authors
check it directly. If each query of Qwen-3.8-27B attends only to its true top 512 keys (plus the
first few tokens and a recent window), the model keeps **98%** of its RULER accuracy at 128k tokens while reading **0.8%** of
the keys. So the layer can be split in two. An *indexer* chooses a fixed budget of k keys per
query, and the attention reads only those, which costs O(Tk) to prefill and O(k) per decoded
token. The attention stops being the problem.

The indexer becomes it. To find the best k keys out of T, the indexers in today's models score all
T of them, or all T/4 blocks of four. That is still quadratic in prefill and linear in decode. The
refinements that have shipped all attack the constant: fewer and smaller indexer heads, lower
precision, compressing every four keys into one before scoring them (DeepSeek's CSA, Qwen's QSA,
GLM-5.3-Flash), reusing one layer's selection in the next (IndexCache, DeepSeek-V4.1). Each divides
the indexer's cost by a constant, and a constant does not hold off a quadratic for long.

Figure 1 shows the point where it stops holding.

Sparse attention did its job. In prefill, the layer is 21–27× faster than full attention at every
length shown. But the indexer's share of what is left climbs from two-thirds at 512k tokens to
98% at 10M, and in decode from 41% to 89%. The authors put a number on the headroom. If the
indexer were free, the layer would prefill a further **58×** faster and decode **8.9×** faster.

This is Amdahl's law in its plainest form: make one part of a job fast enough, and the job becomes
whatever you did not speed up. Sparse attention made reading keys cheap. The cost of a
long-context layer is now the cost of finding them.

## Search the clusters, not the keys

The obvious way to avoid scoring every key is to score summaries of groups of keys, then open only
the promising groups. Block sparse attention already does a version of this. It groups keys by
position, each block holding consecutive tokens, and scores the block. The weakness is the
grouping. Consecutive tokens are neighbours in the text, not in meaning, so a block's summary
averages one relevant key with its unrelated neighbours and can hide it. In the paper, block
search organised as a tree (a training-free baseline) falls to about **63** on RULER at 1M tokens
on both models, and larger blocks fall sooner. Even scanned in full and distilled exactly as LSA
is, block selection scores below LSA on RULER from 128k tokens on Qwen-3.8-27B.

LSA groups keys by content instead. It maps keys into a space where similarity tracks attention
(a learned 64-dimensional projection in the distilled variant, the attention's own keys in the
native one), clusters them there, and lets each query score the cluster centroids. The members of
a cluster resemble each other, so a centroid is a faithful summary of all of them, and a relevant
key's cluster scores well because the key does.

If you have used a vector database, you have seen this before. Cluster the collection, score the
centroids, open only the best clusters: that is the inverted-file index of approximate
nearest-neighbour search, with the attention itself doing the final ranking. LSA builds one inside
every global attention layer, extends it as tokens arrive, and searches it for every query. Figure 2 shows
the whole path, with the values the paper runs.

Three details matter more than they look.

**The index is built incrementally.** Keys are clustered 512 at a time, as each block of 512 fills,
and a block's buckets never change afterwards. The newest keys, not yet clustered, are exactly the
ones the attention window covers, so nothing is ever unreachable and nothing is re-indexed. That is
what makes the scheme usable in decode, where tokens arrive one at a time.

**One index query serves every head.** The query heads are summed before projection, so each token
produces a single list of keys that all heads share. That keeps the search cheap. It also assumes
that one layer's heads mostly want the same keys, which the accuracy results below put to the test.

**The model's attention is untouched.** LSA only changes which keys the attention reads, so
standard kernels do the attending. The paper reuses FlashAttention-3, which reads the selected
positions as if they were a page table.

## Flat search shrinks the constant; tree search changes the exponent

LSA can search its buckets in two ways, and the difference between them is the difference between
the paper's results and its title.

**Flat search** scores every bucket centroid. That is still a scan of the whole context, so flat
search is still quadratic in prefill and linear per decoded token. What shrinks is the constant:
one centroid for about every eight keys, where GLM-5.3-Flash's indexer keeps one index key for
every four, in 64 dimensions instead of 128, scored by a single index query per token. Every
headline number in the paper comes from flat search.

**Tree search** clusters the buckets again into larger buckets, and those again, building a
hierarchy. A query descends it with a beam, keeping the best nodes at each level and expanding only
their children. With a fixed beam, a query scores O(log T) centroids, and prefill becomes
O(T log T). That is the subquadratic attention of the title.

At today's lengths, the tree is not yet the better choice:

- **Prefill.** Flat search stays faster up to 10M tokens. The authors extrapolate that the tree
  overtakes it beyond that, with a prefill more than **90×** faster than baseline sparse attention at
  100M tokens. That is a projection, not a measurement.
- **Decode.** The tree walks its levels one after another, which only pays off when many requests
  decode together. With one request, flat selection is faster up to about 5M tokens. With 4 requests
  the tree wins from about 1M, with 16 from about 256k, and with 16 requests at 10M its selection
  step is **5.6×** faster. The paper benchmarks one request at a time, so every tree result in it
  decodes with flat search.
- **Accuracy.** On GLM-5.3-Flash the tree loses accuracy past 1M tokens: **55.8** on RULER at 10M,
  against **66.8** for flat search.

So the "towards" in the title is honest. The method behind the paper's numbers is a much cheaper
scan. The method that removes the scan is built and measured, and it looks promising, but it is not
yet better.

Why does flat search hold up so well if it is still quadratic? Because at these sizes what is left
of the scan is small. D-LSA (Flat) prefills its last 32,768-query chunk on Qwen-3.8-27B in 154 ms
at 512k tokens and 185 ms at 10M: twenty times the context for a fifth more time. The quadratic
term is still there, but below 10M it no longer dominates.

## Where the latent space comes from

The search needs a space in which "similar" means "relevant". The paper offers two ways to get one.

**Distilled LSA (D-LSA)** retrofits an existing model, which stays frozen. For each attention
layer, D-LSA learns two small projections, one for keys and one for queries, into the
64-dimensional index space, plus a temperature. They are trained so that the softmax of the index
scores matches the layer's own attention, averaged over its heads: a forward KL divergence against
each query's 2,048 most-attended keys. During this training the indexer scores every key directly;
clustering only enters at inference. The run is short: **352M** tokens of documents between 16k
and 1M tokens long, against the **2.1B** tokens of DeepSeek's dense warm-up for its own indexer.
Unlike DeepSeek's recipe, the model is not trained further under sparse attention afterwards. The
paper supports that step but skips it for cost, which matters when reading the accuracy results
below. There is even a training-free version that uses the keys' principal directions as both
projections. It stays close to trained D-LSA on Qwen-3.8-27B and trails it on GLM-5.3-Flash.

**Native LSA (N-LSA)** builds the selection into the model from the start, trained on next-token
prediction alone. It has no index projections: it clusters the attention's own keys. Each
attention layer has a single key-value head, so one key per token serves all eight query heads,
and a bucket scores as the best match any head finds for its centroid. No gradient flows through
the selection, so the loss trains the attention only through the keys each query actually read.
N-LSA adds no parameters and needs no teacher and no auxiliary loss.

## One layer: the speedup grows with the context

The paper times one global attention layer on one GPU, including its projections, the indexer and
the attention. Prefill is the last chunk of 32,768 queries before the given context; decode is one
step of one request.

The speedup is small where the old indexer was still cheap and large where it was not. On
GLM-5.3-Flash, against the model's own sparse attention, prefill gains **2.1×** at 512k tokens,
**3.5×** at 1M and **22.7×** at 10M, and decode goes from no change to **4.6×**. Against full
attention in Qwen-3.8-27B, the 10M figures are **72.4×** in prefill and **42.5×** in decode. In
absolute terms, the last prefill chunk at 10M drops from 13.4 s to 185 ms on Qwen-3.8-27B and from
1.51 s to 66.6 ms on GLM-5.3-Flash. A decode step drops from 11 ms to 260 µs, and from 1.15 ms to
249 µs. On B300 GPUs the shape is the same: 42.9× and 18.4× on Qwen-3.8-27B, 12.5× and 5.2× on
GLM-5.3-Flash.

One detail shows that the search really was the cost. Past 1M tokens, D-LSA on GLM-5.3-Flash
reads **4,096** long-range keys per query, twice the **2,048** that the model's own indexer
selects. It does twice the attention and still finishes the layer 22.7× sooner.

The index is smaller, too. At 10M tokens D-LSA's bucket cache takes 246 MiB per layer, against
331 MiB for GLM-5.3-Flash's indexer and 642 MiB for a QSA-style one. All three sit next to a KV cache of
about 10 GiB per layer on GLM-5.3-Flash and 40 GiB on Qwen-3.8-27B, which LSA does not shrink.

## The whole model: smaller, and only at the far end

A layer is not a model. The paper also serves both models in SGLang on eight GPUs, one request at
a time, and measures time to first token (TTFT) and time per output token (TPOT).

At 10M tokens the gains survive. Qwen-3.8-27B's first token arrives **9.2×** sooner, after about
eight minutes instead of seventy-six (4,582 s with full attention), and each later token comes
**2.9×** faster. GLM-5.3-Flash with context parallelism gets **2.2×** on the first token, 451 s
down to about 200, and **2.1×** per token. With tensor parallelism, where its baseline is slower to
begin with, the figures are **5.8×** and **1.9×**.

The fall from 72.4× for a layer to 9.2× for a model has two causes. Only the global attention
layers get faster. Everything else keeps its cost: the MLPs and experts, and any cheaper attention
layers interleaved with the global ones. And the layer benchmark times the last and
most expensive chunk of the prefill, while a real prefill also runs every earlier chunk, at shorter
contexts where the gain is small.

At 512k tokens there is nothing to collect. First-token speedups run from **0.68×** to **1.22×**
and per-token ones from **0.63×** to **1.01×**. Qwen-3.8-27B on B300 takes about half again as long
to its first token with D-LSA as without it. Even at 1M tokens, GLM-5.3-Flash with context
parallelism is only on par with its baseline. Below a million tokens the old indexer is cheap enough
that a better search has little to save, and LSA's own machinery is not free.

One more comparison is worth making. The paper also distils a QSA-style block-sparse indexer onto
Qwen-3.8-27B, trained exactly as D-LSA's projections are. Against full attention it brings the first
token at 10M **8.0×** sooner, close to D-LSA's **9.2×**, and at 512k and 1M it is the faster of the
two. The decisive gap is per token. At 10M, the block-sparse model decodes slightly *slower* than
full attention (0.89×) while D-LSA decodes **2.9×** faster.

## What it costs in accuracy

Reading fewer keys risks missing the right one. The paper tests both models on knowledge
(MMLU-Pro, GPQA-Diamond), reasoning (AIME25, MATH500) and long context (LongBench v2, RULER up to
10M tokens, and a new benchmark, PaperTrail).

On knowledge and reasoning, every D-LSA variant lands inside the 95% confidence interval of its
baseline, and the length of the reasoning does not measurably change. That is reassuring but weak
evidence, because the intervals are wide. LongBench v2 is 60 questions with an interval of ±11.6
points: D-LSA (Flat) on Qwen-3.8-27B scores 5 points lower and is still "within" it.

On long context the two models diverge.

**Qwen-3.8-27B** stays within 5 points of full attention up to 1M tokens and is ahead at 10M:
**63.9** against **59.9** on RULER, and **29.1** against **19.8** on PaperTrail. Read the RULER
result as "no loss" rather than a gain. Above 1M tokens RULER runs 20 prompts per task, and the lead
comes mostly from two tasks, MultiQuery (92 against 72) and HotpotQA (35 against 20). At 20
prompts a task, those gaps carry the weight of four prompts and three. The full-attention baseline is also running far
outside its range. Qwen-3.8-27B reaches 10M tokens only through YaRN position scaling at a factor
of 40, well beyond its advertised context.

**GLM-5.3-Flash** stays within 3 points of its own sparse attention up to 1M tokens, falls behind
by up to **8** points between 2M and 5M, and comes back to within 4 on RULER at 10M (−3.7). On
PaperTrail it trails by 7.4 points at 10M, mostly on questions that link facts across two or more
papers. This comparison is tilted against D-LSA. GLM-5.3-Flash's indexer was trained together with
the model, while D-LSA was distilled onto a frozen model and never trained further. Whether that
extra step would close the gap is an open question.

Some tasks fail for everyone. MultiKey 2, MultiKey 3 and common-words extraction fall to 5 or less
at 10M tokens for every method, baselines included, which caps every RULER average at that length.
At ten million tokens, these models' long-context retrieval is limited by more than the attention.

PaperTrail deserves a note because the authors built it. It hides a trail of fabricated facts in a
collection of recent papers on exoplanets, long-context machine learning and quantum error
correction, almost all published after the models were released, and asks questions that need
one, two, or three or more of those facts joined up. The design is sensible and includes controls,
such as questions whose answer is not in the corpus. But it is new, and on its hardest tier every
method on both models scores 19 or less at 10M tokens.

## Training it in from the start

The native variant is tested at small scale. The model is a hybrid of about 0.5B parameters with 24
layers, in which every fourth layer is attention and the rest are Gated DeltaNet linear-attention
layers. Each attention variant is pre-trained on 100B tokens of FineWeb-Edu at a 4k context, then
decayed on 12B tokens of long documents at 128k. Every sparse method reads about 2,560 keys per
query. N-LSA reads 2,048 selected keys, a 512-key window and 4 sink keys. NSA reads 32 blocks of 64
plus a 512-key window, PISA 40 blocks of 64, and sliding-window attention its last 2,560 keys.

N-LSA matches full attention's validation loss at 128k exactly, **1.085** to **1.085**, while
PISA, NSA and sliding window trail at 1.100, 1.117 and 1.154. On RULER at 128k it scores **32.2**
against full attention's **34.7**. NSA and PISA fall to 19.2 and 14.6, and sliding window to 3.0
once the context outgrows its window. N-LSA also trains faster. One attention layer's forward and
backward pass is **1.1×** faster than full attention with FlashAttention-3 at 64k and **1.6×** at
128k, and the whole model finishes its decay phase **1.24×** sooner. At shorter contexts the
selection costs more than it saves. Peak memory per layer is also higher, 6.8 GiB against 5.8 at
128k, because the selected indices are kept for the backward pass.

This is the most encouraging result in the paper and the least proven. It is a 0.5B model, trained
to 128k with flat search only, and absolute RULER scores are low for every method at that size.
Whether native clustering holds up at frontier scale and with million-token training is the
obvious next experiment.

## Where it stops

- **It cuts finding, not storing.** The KV cache still grows linearly with the context: 10 GiB per
  layer for GLM-5.3-Flash at 10M tokens. LSA is orthogonal to KV-cache compression, cross-layer
  index sharing and multi-token prediction, and could be combined with each.
- **Every benchmark is one request at a time.** Production serving batches requests, which changes
  the balance between flat and tree search and between the parallelism strategies. LSA also keeps a
  full copy of its index on every GPU, trading memory for communication.
- **The subquadratic part is still a projection.** The tree beats flat search in decode only with
  batching or past about 5M tokens, and in prefill only beyond 10M, by extrapolation.
- **Native training is small.** One model size, one context length, flat search.

## What to do with it

The code is public under Apache 2.0 at
[Prefrontal-AI/latent-sparse-attention](https://github.com/Prefrontal-AI/latent-sparse-attention).
The release includes an SGLang fork (tag `lsa-v0.1.0`, also published as a Docker image), the
distilled index projections for Qwen-3.8-27B and GLM-5.3-Flash, the QSA-style baseline indexer,
checkpoints for all ten native-training runs, and the kit to rebuild PaperTrail. It ships Triton
kernels that run on any GPU and faster CuTe DSL kernels for H200 and B300.

The first candidates are systems that really do hold millions of tokens: coding agents with long
histories, assistants that search large document collections, anything that must join facts across
a corpus. For those:

- **Know your context distribution first.** The gains appear past a million tokens. If most of your
  requests are shorter, a block-sparse indexer is as good or better today, and D-LSA can make short
  requests slower. If you adopt it, switch it on by context length.
- **Measure both latencies, at your batch size.** First-token and per-token gains differ, sometimes
  by a lot, and the paper's numbers are for one request at a time.
- **Compare against your strongest sparse baseline, not against full attention.** The 72.4× and
  9.2× figures are against full attention. Against a good block-sparse indexer, the first-token gain
  at 10M is small and the real gain is in decode.
- **Test the tasks you care about.** Multi-key retrieval fails first, for every method. If
  distilling onto your frozen model costs accuracy, the sparse-training step the paper skipped is
  the next lever to pull.

The larger point will outlast this particular method. For years, long-context research asked how
to make attention cheaper. Sparse attention answered that, and in doing so turned it into a search
problem: given a query, find the few thousand keys out of ten million that matter, faster than
reading them all. Vector search has worked on that problem for two decades. LSA borrows its oldest
answer (cluster, score the centroids, open the best clusters) and adds a tree for the scale still
to come. Expect the next round of long-context work to look less like attention research and more
like index engineering.
